rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening matches al-Ṭūr’s close in wording through the shared star reference and in meaning: its night-and-stars conclusion leads into the staged account of the Prophet’s opponents.
rows.anchor: أول هذه السورة مناسب لآخر ما قبلها لفظا ومعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prior oath sūras establish divine oneness, resurrection and recompense, and lasting punishment; this sūra’s oath establishes prophethood, completing the three foundations.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه السورة لنبوة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لتكمل الأصول الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an swears less often for oneness and prophethood because their signs are rational or widely transmitted, but stresses resurrection because revelation alone establishes its occurrence decisively.
rows.anchor: فلا يمكن إثباته إلا بالسمع فأكثر القسم ليقطع به المكلف

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some exegetes distinguish ḍalāl as the opposite of guidance and ghayy as the opposite of right conduct; Rāzī says most commentators do not distinguish them.
rows.anchor: الضلال في مقابلة الهدى ، والغي في مقابلة الرشد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says ḍalāl is broader in ordinary usage: a traveler may lose every route to a destination, while ghayy describes having no straight route; hence a sinner may be foolish or unrighteous without being called astray.
rows.anchor: الضلال أعم استعمالا في الوضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this distinction, “he did not stray” denies unbelief, while “he did not go astray” denies even the lesser fault of sinful conduct; Rāzī also compares ḍalāl to nonexistence and ghayy to corrupt existence.
rows.anchor: ولا أقل من ذلك فما فسق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Rāzī ranks ḍalāl like nonexistence and ghayy like corrupt existence.
rows.anchor: كالوجود الفاسد في الدرجة والمرتبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Your ṣāḥib” can mean your master or your companion.
rows.anchor: وجهان الأول : سيدكم والآخر : مصاحبكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī allows “did not stray” to mean “was not insane,” since a madman is described as astray; he links the denial to the assurance that the Prophet is a wise guide to God.
rows.anchor: فإن المجنون ضال ، وعلى هذا فهو كقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence presents him as on the right path, then on a straight path, then as swiftly following its course; alternatively, not speaking from desire proves he cannot be led astray by desire.
rows.anchor: قال أولا { ما ضل } أي هو على الطريق { وما غوى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past-tense denials can describe the Prophet’s protected earlier life, including his childhood and retreat; his present speech is now revelation that rescues and guides others.
rows.anchor: وصار الآن منقذا من الضلالة ومرشدا وهاديا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God preserves someone destined for prophethood from unbelief and grave vices in youth; Rāzī applies this protection to the Prophet’s earlier life.
rows.anchor: يصون من يريد إرساله في صغره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī treats hawā here as the soul’s base appetite: its letters suggest falling and lowliness, and Qur’anic usage sets it against praiseworthy love; he cites the soul restrained from desire.
rows.anchor: لم يستعمل الهوى إلا في المواضع الذي يخالف المحبة

none: bare heading and verse text only

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators take the pronoun in “he taught him” to refer to the revelation: the mighty in power taught the revelation, whether it is scripture or inspiration.
rows.anchor: الضمير في { علمه } عائدا إلى الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers that the pronoun refers to Muhammad: Gabriel, the mighty in power, taught the Prophet, the “companion” mentioned earlier; Gabriel’s intellectual and practical faculties are strong.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن يقال الضمير عائد إلى محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم تقديره علم محمد شديد القوى جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praising the teacher also praises the student, making Muhammad’s distinction visible in a way that merely naming Gabriel as teacher would not.
rows.anchor: أن مدح المعلم مدح المتعلم فلو قال علمه جبريل ولم يصفه ما كان يحصل للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فضيلة ظاهرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Gabriel mighty answers the opponents’ claim that Muhammad heard ancient tales during a trip to Syria: his teacher was no ordinary human.
rows.anchor: فيه ردا عليهم حيث قالوا أساطير الأولين سمعها وقت سفره إلى الشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel’s perceptive power, memory, and integrity together warrant trust in his transmission, just as the description of the messenger in al-Takwīr combines strength, standing, and trustworthiness.
rows.anchor: قوة الإدراك شرط الوثوق بقول القائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description consoles Muhammad: Gabriel can withstand divine communication; God may first teach through an intermediary and then directly, as in “He taught you what you did not know.”
rows.anchor: في تسلية النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

none: bare heading and verse text only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading is that God revealed to Muhammad what He had revealed to Gabriel, either by addressing him that it was revelation or by creating necessary knowledge in him.
rows.anchor: أوحى إلى محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم ما أوحاه إلى جبريل أي كلمه الله أنه وحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading is that God gave Gabriel the proof by which he recognized the message to Muhammad as revelation; on this reading mā is a verbal noun, distinguishing an angel from a jinn.
rows.anchor: أوحى إلى جبريل ما أوحى إلى محمد دليله الذي به يعرف أنه وحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question challenges why the opponents dispute and raise doubts when the Prophet saw directly and with certainty; seeing leaves him sure, despite their allegation that jinn had afflicted him.
rows.anchor: أي كيف تجادلونه وتوردون شكوككم عليه مع أنه رأى ما رأى عين اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī also reads the statement as emphasis: even a certain person may still face doubts he cannot answer, but inability to answer does not undo certainty.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن من تيقن شيئا قد يكون بحيث لا يزول عن نفسه تشكيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first sight on earth left only a remote possibility that the figure was a jinn, despite Muhammad’s necessary knowledge that he was an angel; seeing him at the Sidra above the sixth heaven excludes jinn or human presence.
rows.anchor: فلما رآه عند سدرة المنتهى وهو فوق السماء السادسة لم يحتمل أن يكون هناك جن ولا إنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī allows the wāw in the question to coordinate or introduce a circumstantial clause: how can they dispute what he saw when he saw it without doubt?
rows.anchor: المسألة الأولى : الواو يحتمل أن تكون عاطفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A certain person may still be unable to answer skeptical objections; Rāzī compares this to certainty that seas and mountains persisted during sleep despite an unanswerable hypothetical objection.
rows.anchor: لا نشك في أن البحار ما صارت ذهبا والجبال ما صارت عهنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām does not preclude a circumstantial wāw: a circumstantial clause may be nominal or verbal, and either can include the lām.
rows.anchor: الواو التي للحال تدخل على جملة والجملة تتركب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nazlatan is a verbal noun on the faʿla pattern from descending, so an agent must have descended; the identity of the pronoun in “he saw him” determines the options.
rows.anchor: فعلة من النزول فهي كجلسة من الجلوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the pronoun refers to God, following the interpretation of “what he saw” in 53:11, Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice.
rows.anchor: في قوله { ما كذب الفؤاد ما رأى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed sense is God’s physical movement or relocation; Rāzī rejects this as false.
rows.anchor: قول من يجوز على الله تعالى الحركة والانتقال وهو باطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other proposed sense is nonphysical nearness: God draws his servant near through mercy and favor, without the servant seeing him.
rows.anchor: فإن الله تعالى قد يقرب بالرحمة والفضل من عبده ولا يراه العبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the view that Muhammad saw God, Rāzī offers the image of the Prophet descending on the mount of passion and the vehicle of the self.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم نزل على متن الهوى ومركب النفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “descent” can stand for ascent’s opposite, marking the event as the worldly ascent, which has a return, unlike the ascent of the hereafter.
rows.anchor: أن المراد من النزلة ضدها وهي العرجة كأنه قال رآه عرجة أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second major view takes the pronoun as Gabriel: Muhammad saw Gabriel during another descent.
rows.anchor: أنه عائد إلى جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī cites an account of the Night Journey: Muhammad passed beyond Gabriel, who said that advancing a finger further would burn him, then returned to Gabriel; this is one explanation of the descent.
rows.anchor: وقال له جبريل عليه السلام لو دنوت أنملة لاحترقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return may be called “another” because Muhammad repeatedly passed Gabriel and descended back to him during the repeated trips concerning prayer.
rows.anchor: لأن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في أمر الصلاة تردد مرارا فربما كان يجاوز كل مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the descent belongs to Gabriel, who descended to Muhammad twice while appearing in his own form.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون لجبريل عليه السلام وكلاهما منقول وعلى هذا الوجه فنزلة أخرى ظاهر

rows.speaker: المشهور
rows.claim: The famous view places the Sidrat al-Muntahā in the seventh heaven; another report places it in the sixth.
rows.anchor: المشهور أن السدرة شجرة في السماء السابعة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet describes the tree’s fruit as jars from Hajar and its leaves as elephant ears; Rāzī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: نيقها كقلال هجر وورقها كآذان الفيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss makes the Sidra the utmost bewilderment, beyond which there is no bewilderment; Muhammad did not become bewildered or absent.
rows.anchor: وقيل سدرة المنتهى هي الحيرة القصوى من السدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “At” may denote place, meaning near the Sidra, or time, meaning the moment when the minds of the wise are at their most bewildered, though Muhammad was not bewildered then.
rows.anchor: المشهور أنه ظرف مكان تقديره رأى جبريل أو غيره بقرب سدرة المنتهى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the pronoun means God, reading “at the Sidra” as God’s location in a place is false; it can instead describe Muhammad as the one who was at the Sidra when he saw.
rows.anchor: قول من يجعل الله في مكان وهو باطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the referent is Gabriel, either account of “at the Sidra” works, but Rāzī says Muhammad being there with Gabriel is clearer.
rows.anchor: وكون النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مع جبريل عند سدرة المنتهى أظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive may attach the tree to its place: the endpoint is a place no angel, or even spirit, passes beyond.
rows.anchor: إضافة الشيء إلى مكانه يقال أشجار بلدة كذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the genitive attaches a locus to what is in it: the tree is at the endpoint of knowledge.
rows.anchor: إضافة المحل إلى الحال فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading makes it a possessive construction with the endpoint to God understood; association with God honors the tree.
rows.anchor: إضافة الملك إلى مالكه يقال دار زيد وأشجار زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article may identify Muhammad’s sight: if locusts and moths covered the Sidra, he did not turn to them or lose sight of his purpose; their covering the tree tests him.
rows.anchor: المعروف وهو بصر محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If divine lights covered the Sidra, Muhammad neither looked aside nor became unconscious, unlike Moses; the readings display his composure and strength.
rows.anchor: فإنه قطع النظر وغشي عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the article is generic: no sight at all veered under the awe. Rāzī answers that generic scope can also be expressed by a definite noun under negation, as in 6:103.
rows.anchor: في اللام أنه لتعريف الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning sight rather than heart shows that the encounter was immense while Muhammad’s sight remained steady without involuntary deviation, like a composed person before a king.
rows.anchor: يحصل منه فائدة أن الأمر كان عظيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause may be an independent sentence or have an omitted subject supplied from the first clause.
rows.anchor: جملة مستقلة على جملة أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With locusts or moths, Muhammad looked neither at them nor at anything besides God; with divine lights, he neither turned from the lights nor sought beyond them.
rows.anchor: ولا إلى غير الجراد سوى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word choice “deviate” and “transgress” marks looking aside or beyond as blameworthy in that setting; it also portrays Muhammad’s arrival at unsurpassed certainty.
rows.anchor: الميل في ذلك الموضع والمجاوزة مذمومان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī also reads the sight as neither straying from the way nor perceiving things contrary to their reality, nor imagining something nonexistent as real.
rows.anchor: فلم ير الشيء على خلاف ما هو عليه

none: bare heading and verse text only
bare heading and verse text only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clearest antecedent for “that” is conjecture: the farthest these people reach in knowledge is reliance on conjecture.
rows.anchor: غاية ما يبلغون به أنهم يأخذون بالظن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second possibility is that preferring worldly life is the limit of their knowledge.
rows.anchor: إيثار الحياة الدنيا مبلغهم من العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third possibility takes “that” to mean the turning away described just before; here “knowledge” means the known thing, the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وذلك الإعراض غاية ما بلغوه من العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī describes responses to the Qur’an from highest to lowest: wholehearted acceptance, acceptance of its miracle and following the Messenger, hesitation such as Abū Ṭālib’s, and rejection with blame.
rows.anchor: بعضهم تلقاه بالقبول وانشرح صدره فبلغ الغاية القصوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although one might object that God does not burden beyond capacity and a child or mad person lacks knowledge, Rāzī says their ignorance followed their turning away from remembrance, so it grounds their punishment.
rows.anchor: عدم علمهم لعدم قبولهم العلم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats 53:30 as an interruption; the connected sequence runs from the command to turn away from those who abandon remembrance to God’s knowledge of the astray.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري : { ذلك مبلغهم من العلم } كلام معترض بين كلامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī argues the central statement is needed to explain the command: leave them because this is the utmost they attain; their turning away and preference for the immediate explain their ignorance.
rows.anchor: المقصود لا يتم إلا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: First, the Prophet hoped reminders would win more of his people without fighting; God’s knowledge of who is guided or astray means debate should give way to fighting, and removes uncertainty or despair about the outcome.
rows.anchor: علم أنه يؤمن بمجرد الدعاء أحد من المكلفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Second, as in 34:24 and 7:87, opponents claimed guidance despite the Prophet’s proof; he should leave the judgment to God, like litigants before a powerful king who knows the truth.
rows.anchor: وإنا أو إياكم لعلى هدى أو فى ضلال مبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Third, the Prophet had endured serious harm hoping they would believe; since they did not, God’s knowledge of misled and guided people assures recompense for evil and good.
rows.anchor: لله ما في السموات والأرض ليجزي الذين أساؤوا بما عملوا ويجزي الذين أحسنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun huwa is an ʿimād or faṣl. Though the sentence is complete without it, it prevents a hearer from wondering whether “most knowing” is the predicate or part of a following clause.
rows.anchor: يسمى عمادا وفصلا ، ولو قال
